The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with the good tidings, they said, "Peace!" He said, "Peace"﴾.

This noble verse indicates that Abraham returned the greeting to the angels. And there has come in Surah Al-Hijr what gives the impression that when they greeted him, he answered them by being fearful of them without returning the greeting, and that is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "Peace!" He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you"﴾ [Al-Hijr: 52].

The answer is clear, and it is that Abraham answered them with both matters: returning the greeting, and informing them of his fear of them. One of them is mentioned in Hud and the other in Al-Hijr. This is indicated by His mention, in Surah Adh-Dhariyat, of what indicates both together, in His saying: ﴿They said, "Peace!" He said, "Peace, [you are] a people unknown"﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 25], because His saying "unknown" (munkarun) indicates his fear of them. This is clarified by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But he felt a fear of them﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 28], in Hud and Adh-Dhariyat, although in each of the two he said: "Peace."

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 72:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this, my husband, is an old man? Indeed, this is an amazing thing!"﴾.

Allah, may He be exalted and high, explained in this noble surah what the wife of Ibrahim said when she was given the good news of a child while she was an old woman (p-187). He did not explain here what she did at that moment, but He explained what she did in "adh-Dhariyat" (The Scatterers) with His saying: ﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry, and she struck her face and said, "An old barren woman!"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 29]. His saying ﴿in a loud cry﴾ means in an outcry and a shout, and His saying ﴿she struck her face﴾ means she slapped it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the good tidings had come to Ibrahim, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lut﴾, he did not specify here what Ibrahim argued with the angels about concerning the people of Lut. However, he alluded to it in "al-'Ankabut" with His saying: ﴿They said, "Indeed, we will destroy the people of this town; indeed, its people have been wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, in it is Lut." They said, "We are most knowing of who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife"﴾ – the verse [al-'Ankabut: 31, 32].

So the substance of his argument with them was that he was saying: if you destroy the town while there is in it a believer, you will be destroying that believer without a sin. They answered him concerning this with their saying ﴿We are most knowing of who is in it﴾ – the verse [al-'Ankabut: 32].

A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers﴾ ﴿But We did not find in it except one house of Muslims﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 35, 36].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 76:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Ibrahim, turn away from this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, there is coming upon them a punishment that cannot be turned back.﴾

This punishment, which He here declared will inevitably come upon the people of Lut and that cannot be averted, He explained in several places, such as His saying in this noble surah: ﴿So when Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon it stones of hard clay, layered, [marked] from your Lord. And it is not far from the wrongdoers.﴾ [Hud: 82, 83].

And His saying in "al-Hijr": ﴿So We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon them stones of hard clay.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern.﴾ [al-Hijr: 74, 75].

And His saying: ﴿And they had already passed by the city upon which a rain of evil had been rained﴾ [al-Furqan: 40], the verse [in full].

And His saying: ﴿Then We destroyed the others, and We rained upon them a rain, and evil was the rain of those who were warned.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 172, 173].

And His saying: ﴿to send down upon them stones of clay, marked in the sight of your Lord for the transgressors.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 33, 34], and other verses besides these.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 77:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed for them and felt helplessness over them and said, "This is a trying day."﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, majestic and exalted, mentions that when Lot, upon him and our Prophet be blessings and peace, was visited by the messengers of his Lord from among the angels, their coming caused him great distress, and his chest was constricted by it. In several places He indicates that the cause of his distress and of his being "constricted for them" and saying "This is a trying day" was that he thought they were guests from among the children of Adam, as Abraham, upon them both be blessings and peace, had thought. He also thought that his people would violate the sanctity of his guests and commit upon them the abomination of sodomy (liwāṭ). For if they learned of the arrival of a guest, they would rejoice and be glad at him, in order to commit the aforementioned abomination upon him. Among this is His saying here: ﴿And his people came rushing to him, and before this they had been doing evil deeds. He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a man of reason?"﴾ ﴿They said, "You already know that we have no right to your daughters, and indeed you know what we want."﴾ [Hud: 78, 79].

And His saying in "al-Hijr": ﴿And the people of the city came rejoicing.﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, these are my guests, so do not shame me.﴾ ﴿And fear Allah and do not disgrace me."﴾ ﴿They said, "Did we not forbid you from [protecting] the worlds?"﴾ ﴿He said, "These are my daughters, if you must act."﴾ ﴿By your life, indeed they were in their intoxication, wandering blindly.﴾ [al-Hijr: 67–72].

As for His saying "yuhra‘ūn" [Hud: 78], it means they hasten and run from their joy at that. From this is the verse of Muhalhil:

*They came "yuhra‘ūn" while they were captives, led by them against the will of the noses* (i.e., in humiliation).

As for His saying "wa lā tukhzūn" [do not disgrace me], it means: do not humiliate me or debase me by violating the sanctity of my guest. Its noun form is *al-khizy*, with a kasra on the kha' and a sukun on the zay. From this is the verse of Hassan concerning ‘Utbah ibn Abi Waqqas:

*So may my Lord disgrace you, O ‘Utaybah ibn Malik, and may He meet you, before death, with one of the thunderbolts.*

Some scholars said: His saying "wa lā tukhzūn" [al-Hijr: 69] is from *al-khazāya*, which is shame and bashfulness at disgrace; that is, do not do to my guest what would be a cause of my shame and embarrassment. From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah describing a wild bull being chased by dogs along the edge of a sand dune:

*Until, when it circled in the earth, pride returned it, and had it wished, flight would have saved its soul.*

*A disgrace overtook it after its wandering, from the side of the dune, with anger mixed into it.*

He means that this bull, had it wished, could have escaped the dogs by fleeing, but it was too proud and disdained to flee, so it turned back toward them. From this is another verse:

*Shall you make the mother of al-Thuwayr a disgrace upon me, because I fled when I met the Banu ‘Abs?*

Its verb is *khaziya yakhza*, like *radiya yarda*. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Of the fair ones who do not feel disgrace when the wind blows her veil about and her necklace slips from her neck.*

And the saying of another:

*Indeed I do not feel disgrace when it is said of me that I am poor yet generous, but I feel disgrace that it be said I am miserly.*

As for His saying "la‘amruka" [by your life, al-Hijr: 72]: its meaning is "I swear by your life." Allah, exalted is He, has the right to swear by whatever He wills of His creation. He did not swear in the Qur'an by the life of anyone except our Prophet (ﷺ), and in that there is an honour for him (ﷺ) that is not hidden.

It is not permissible for any created being to swear by other than Allah, due to His (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever is going to swear, let him swear by Allah or let him remain silent."

As for His saying "la‘amruka" — it is a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is omitted; that is, "By your life is my oath." It has been heard from the Arabs that they place the rā' before the lām in *la‘amruka*, so they say *ra‘amlaka*. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Ra‘amlaka, indeed the flying bird that came upon me from a bird is truthful.*

As for His saying "la-fī sakratihim" [al-Hijr: 72]: it means their blindness, ignorance and misguidance. *Al-‘amah* is blindness of the heart. So the meaning of *ya‘mahūn* [al-Hijr: 72] is that they wander, bewildered, not knowing truth from falsehood, beneficial from harmful, or good from evil.

The scholars differed concerning the intended meaning of Lot's saying, upon him and our Prophet be blessings and peace: ﴿These are my daughters﴾ [Hud: 78], in both places, into several opinions:

The first: that he intended only to defend his guest, and did not intend to carry out what he said. This is the view of ‘Ikrimah and Abu ‘Ubaydah.

The second: that by "daughters" he meant his own daughters by blood, and that the meaning is: leave the abomination of sodomy, and I will marry my daughters to you. On this view, marrying a disbelieving man to a Muslim woman was permissible in his law, just as the daughters of our Prophet (ﷺ) were married to disbelievers at the beginning of Islam, as is well known. Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), sent her necklace, with which her mother Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, may Allah be pleased with her, had adorned her at her wedding to her husband Abu al-‘As ibn al-Rabi‘, to him as ransom for her husband Abu al-‘As, mentioned above, when the Muslims captured him as a disbeliever on the day of Badr. The story is well known, and Shaykh Ahmad al-Badawi al-Shinqiti set it down in his *Maghazi* with his saying about the Battle of Badr:

*And Ibn al-Rabi‘, the son-in-law of the guide of the community, when for his ransom Zaynab sent her necklace, with which Khadijah had gifted her and adorned her. He sent her back with her necklace and with a covenant to him that he return her to her tomorrow, etc.*

The third view: that by "daughters" is meant all the women of his people, because the prophet of a people is a spiritual father to them, (ﷺ) as His saying concerning our Prophet (ﷺ) indicates: ﴿The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka‘b: "and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them," and something similar was narrated from Ibn ‘Abbas. Many scholars held this view.

This view is supported by one indication and weakened by another. As for the indication that supports it: the daughters of Lot could not accommodate all the men of his people, as is clear. So if he were to marry them to men equal in number to them, the majority of his people's men would remain without wives, and it is therefore necessary that the intended meaning be all the women of his people. This generality is supported by His saying: ﴿Do you approach males from among the worlds﴾ ﴿and leave what your Lord has created for you of your wives?﴾ [al-Shu‘ara’: 165, 166], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you approach men with desire instead of women﴾ [al-Naml: 55], and similar verses.

As for the indication that weakens it: the Prophet is not a father to disbelieving women. Rather, the spiritual fatherhood of the prophets is for the believers, not the disbelievers, as His saying indicates: ﴿The Prophet is more worthy of the believers﴾ — the verse [al-Ahzab: 6].

And in *al-Dhariyat* Allah, exalted is He, has explicitly stated that there was no Muslim among the people of Lot except one household, and they were the household of Lot. This is in His saying: ﴿And We found there no house other than a house of Muslims﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 36].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 80:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a strong support."﴾ ﴿They said, "O Lut, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you."﴾.

In this noble verse, Allah, exalted is He, mentions that His prophet Lut admonished his people and forbade them from disgracing him regarding his guests. He also offered them the women in place of the men, but they did not heed his words and persisted in what they were doing of desiring the abomination. So Lut said: ﴿If only I had power against you...﴾ [Hud: 80], and the angels informed him that they were messengers of his Lord, and that the wicked disbelievers would not reach him with any harm.

In al-Qamar, He made clear that He obliterated their eyes, and that is in His statement: ﴿And they had already sought to make him give up his guests, so We blinded their eyes, "Taste then My punishment and warnings."﴾ [al-Qamar: 37].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 81:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So travel with your family in a part of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife. Indeed, what strikes them will strike her.﴾ In this noble verse, He mentioned that He commanded His prophet Lut to travel with his family during a part of the night. He did not specify here whether it was the last part of the night, its middle, or its beginning. However, He specified in "al-Qamar" that it was the last part of the night, at the time of pre-dawn (al-sahar), and that is in His saying: ﴿Except the family of Lut; We saved them at pre-dawn﴾ [al-Qamar: 34]. He also did not specify here that He commanded him to be behind them while they were in front of him. However, He specified that in "al-Hijr" with His saying: ﴿So travel with your family in a part of the night, and follow behind them, and let none of you look back, and proceed where you are commanded﴾ [al-Hijr: 65]. As for His saying: ﴿and let none of you look back, except your wife﴾ [Hud: 81], the majority of reciters read "illa imra'ataka" with a fatha (accusative), and according to this the matter is clear, because it is an exception from "family" (ahl), i.e., travel with your family except your wife, so do not travel with her, and leave her with her people, for she is destroyed along with them.

This reading is supported by His saying about her in several places: ﴿She was among those who remained behind﴾ [al-Ankabut: 32, 33], and "al-ghabir" means "the remaining," i.e., among those who remain in destruction.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "illa imra'atuka" with a damma (nominative), as a substitute (badal) for "ahad." According to this, the meaning is that He commanded Lut to forbid all his family from looking back, except his wife, for it was revealed to him that she would certainly perish, and there is no benefit in forbidding her from looking back since she is among those who will be destroyed.

According to the majority's reading, he did not travel with her. The apparent meaning of the reading of Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir is that he did travel with her, and she looked back and perished.

Some scholars said: When she heard the thunderous roar of the punishment, she looked back and said, "Oh, my people!" So a stone overtook her and killed her.

The author, may Allah pardon him, says: The apparent way of reconciling the two mentioned readings is that the purpose of Lut's command to travel with his family is salvation from the punishment that befell the people of Lut at dawn, and Lut's wife was certainly going to be struck by that punishment which struck her people. Thus, the result of Lut's traveling with his family did not include his wife under either reading, and what has no benefit is like nonexistence. So the meaning that he left her and did not travel with her at all, and the meaning that he traveled with her and she perished with the destroyed, are equivalent.

Thus the meaning of both readings returns to the fact that she is destined for destruction, and traveling with Lut did not benefit her. There is therefore no difference between her remaining with them or leaving and being struck by what struck them.

Since traveling with Lut did not save her from the punishment, she and whoever did not travel with him are equal. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying: ﴿So travel with your family﴾ [Hud: 81], Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "fasri" with a hamzat wasl (connecting hamza), from sara yasri. The majority of reciters read ﴿fa-asri bi-ahlika﴾ with a hamzat qat' (cutting hamza), from asra (the quadriliteral form) on the pattern af'ala. Sara and asra are two dialects and two authentic seven-canonical readings. From the triliteral sara comes His saying: ﴿And the night when it travels﴾ [al-Fajr: 4], for the fatha on the ya' of yasri indicates that it is the present tense of the triliteral sara.

The poet Nabigha Dhubyani combined the two dialects:

"Asrat 'alayhi min al-Jawza'i sariyatun / tuzjī al-shamālu 'alayhā jāmida al-baradi"

He says "asrat" in the quadriliteral form, in the more widely known transmission of the verse, and "sariyatun" is the active participle of the triliteral sara. Another poet also combined them:

"Hatta al-Nadiratu rabbata al-khidri / asrat ilayka wa lam takun tasri"

With a fatha on the ta' of "tasri." Both dialects are very common in the speech of the Arabs. The verbal noun of the quadriliteral is al-isra' by regular pattern, and the verbal noun of the triliteral is al-sura with a damma, on the pattern fu'al with a damma then fatha, which is irregular. From it is the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha:

"Inda al-sabahi yahmadu al-qawmu al-sura / wa tanjali 'anhum ghayabatu al-kara"

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾.

In this noble verse He mentioned that the appointed time for the destruction of the people of Lut was the morning of that night. He said likewise in "al-Hijr," with His saying: ﴿And We conveyed to him that matter, that the last remnant of these would be cut off at morning﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. In "al-Hijr" He added that the morning of the punishment fell upon them at the time of ishraq, which is the time of sunrise, with His saying: ﴿So the shout seized them at sunrise﴾.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of sijjil﴾ [the verse].

The scholars differed greatly regarding the meaning of "stones of sijjil" (sijjil: a hard, baked clay, or a term whose meaning is debated). The apparent meaning is that they were stones of clay of the utmost hardness and strength. The evidence that the meaning of sijjil is clay is His saying, may He be exalted, in "adh-Dhariyat," concerning this very same story: ﴿That We may send down upon them stones of clay﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for those who transgress﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 33, 34]. And the best way to interpret the Qur'an is by the Qur'an (tafsir al-Qur'an bil-Qur'an: interpreting the Qur'an by the Qur'an). The evidence of their strength and severity is that Allah did not punish them with them while He was angry with them except because the punishment by them is far-reaching and severe. Also, some scholars said: sijjil and sijjin are two siblings, both meaning the severe kind of stones and striking. From this is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

"And a band of men who strike the helmets, in the forenoon, with a blow that the champions enjoined upon one another, sijjin."

Based on this, the meaning of ﴿of sijjil﴾ is: of clay of extreme strength. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

**The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah Hud, verse 83**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers.﴾

Scholars have given three interpretations of this noble verse. Two of them are both supported by the Qur'an, and one appears to be weak.

As for the one that appears weak, it is that the meaning is: those stones were not far from the people of Lot, that is, they did not miss them. This was said by al-Qurtubi and others, because this is already covered by Allah's words ﴿And We rained down upon it stones﴾ [Hud: 82] and similar verses.

As for the two interpretations that each have Qur'anic support:

The first is that the dwellings of the people of Lot are not far from the disbelievers who deny our Prophet. They should take warning from what befell its inhabitants when they pass by them on their journeys to al-Sham, and fear that Allah may bring upon them, because they deny our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), the same punishment that fell upon those people because they denied Lot (peace be upon him). The verses indicating this are very numerous.

Such as His saying: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning, and by night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Saffat: 137-138];

And His saying: ﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains. Surely in that is a sign for the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 76-77];

And His saying: ﴿And We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 37];

And His saying: ﴿And We have certainly left of it a clear sign for a people who reason﴾ [al-Ankabut: 35].

And other verses besides these. According to this view, the pronoun in His saying "and it is not" refers to the dwellings of the people of Lot, which is understood from the context.

The second interpretation is that the meaning is: those stones that were rained upon the people of Lot are not far from the wrongdoers who commit deeds like theirs. So it is a warning to the polytheists of the Arabs, like the one before it.

Among the verses indicating this interpretation is His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen what was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers are the like thereof﴾ [Muhammad: 10]. His saying "and for the disbelievers are the like thereof" is very clearly evident in this regard, and verses of this kind are numerous.

**A Note**

The scholars differed regarding the punishment of the one who commits the abomination of the people of Lot. We will mention, if Allah wills, the statements of the scholars on this matter, their evidences, and what appears to be the stronger view on the basis of evidence. So we say, and in Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, we seek help:

Some scholars said: The ruling in this matter is that both the doer and the one to whom it is done are to be killed, absolutely, whether both are married (muhsan) or both are unmarried (bikr), or one is married and the other unmarried.

Among those who held this view are Malik ibn Anas and his companions, one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i, and one of the two narrations from Ahmad. More than one scholar related a consensus (ijma') of the Companions on this view, except that its proponents differed about the manner of killing the one who commits that abomination.

Some of them said: he is to be killed by the sword.

Some of them said: he is to be stoned.

Some of them said: he is to be burned with fire.

Some of them said: he is to be raised atop the highest building in the town, then thrown down headfirst, and stones are to be thrown after him.

The proof of those who say that both the doer and the one to whom it is done in sodomy (liwat) are to be killed absolutely is what was narrated by Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whomever you find doing the deed of the people of Lot, kill the doer and the one to whom it is done."

Ibn Hajar said: Its narrators are trustworthy, except that there is disagreement concerning it.

As for what Yahya ibn Ma'in mentioned, that Amr ibn Abi Amr, the freedman of al-Muttalib, is criticized for this hadith of Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, the response is that this Amr is trustworthy, and the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and Malik narrated from him, as we have mentioned in full earlier.

This hadith is reinforced by what Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning an unmarried man found committing sodomy: that he is to be stoned. This was recorded by Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and al-Bayhaqi.

Also by what al-Hakim and Ibn Majah recorded from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Kill the doer and the one to whom it is done, whether they are married or not." Al-Shawkani said: Its isnad is weak.

Ibn al-Tallaa' said in his book on rulings: It has not been established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he stoned anyone for sodomy, nor that he judged concerning it. But it is established from him that he said: "Kill the doer and the one to whom it is done," which was narrated from him by Ibn Abbas and Abu Hurayrah. End.

The Hafiz said: The hadith of Abu Hurayrah is not sound. It was recorded by al-Bazzar through the chain of Asim ibn Umar al-Umari, from Suhayl, from his father, from him, and Asim is abandoned (matruk). Ibn Majah also narrated it through this route with the wording: "Stone the higher and the lower." End.

Al-Bayhaqi also recorded from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he stoned a man guilty of sodomy. Then he said: al-Shafi'i said: "And according to this we take: stoning the sodomite, whether he is married or not."

And he said: This is the view of Ibn Abbas. He said: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib used to say: the Sunnah is that the sodomite is to be stoned, whether he is married or not.

Al-Bayhaqi also said: Abu Nasr ibn Qatadah and Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Farisi informed us, both saying: Abu Amr ibn Matar related to us, Ibrahim ibn Ali related to us, Yahya ibn Yahya related to us, Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Hazim informed us, Dawud ibn Bakr informed us, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Safwan ibn Sulaym, that Khalid ibn al-Walid wrote to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with both of them, during his caliphate, mentioning to him that he had found a man in some region of the Arabs being mounted as a woman is mounted. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, gathered the people from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked them about it. Among the most severe in opinion that day was Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "This is a sin that no nation among the nations committed except one nation, and Allah did with them what you know. We think he should be burned with fire." So the opinion of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed that he should be burned with fire, and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote to Khalid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him, ordering him to burn him with fire. This is a mursal report.

It was also narrated by another route from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, in a different incident, that he said: He is to be stoned and burned with fire.

And it is mentioned from Ibn Abi Layla, from a man of Hamdan, that Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, stoned a married man for the deed of the people of Lot. Thus al-Thawri mentioned it from him, restricted to the married case, while Hushaym narrated it from Ibn Abi Layla without restriction. End of his words verbatim.

These are the proofs of those who say the doer and the one to whom it is done in sodomy are to be killed.

The proof of those who say that this killing is by fire is what we mentioned earlier from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The proof of those who say that his killing is by the sword is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Kill the doer and the one to whom it is done," and killing, when mentioned without qualification, is understood as killing by the sword.

The proof of those who say that his killing is by stoning is what we have already presented from the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid from Ibn Abbas that he is to be stoned, and what al-Bayhaqi and others mentioned from Ali, that he stoned a sodomite. It is also supported by the fact that Allah rained down upon the people of that abomination stones of sijjil.

The proof of those who say he is to be raised atop the highest building or a mountain, thrown down headfirst, and stones thrown after him, is that this is what the Wise, the All-Aware, did to the people of Lot, as He said: ﴿We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon it stones of baked clay﴾.

The one who wrote these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: This last view is not evident, because the punishment of the people of Lot was not for sodomy alone, but for it and for disbelief and denial of their Prophet (ﷺ). They had combined with sodomy something greater than sodomy, namely disbelief in Allah and harming His Messenger (ﷺ).

The second view: that sodomy is fornication (zina), so the one who commits it is to be flogged one hundred times if he is unmarried and exiled for a year, and stoned if he is married. This view is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

Al-Bayhaqi mentioned from al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman that al-Shafi'i returned to the view that sodomy is zina, so the ruling of zina applies to it. It is also one of the two narrations from Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on them all.

Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it from Ata' and Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It is the view of Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Nakha'i, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, and others.

Those who hold this view argue with what al-Bayhaqi narrated from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from Ibn Sirin, from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When a man mounts a man, they are two adulterers, and when a woman mounts a woman, they are two adulteresses." Abu Abd Allah al-Hafiz informed us, Abu al-Abbas ibn Ya'qub related to us, Yahya ibn Abi Talib related to us, Abu Badr related to us, Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman related to us, and he mentioned it. The Shaykh said: I do not know this Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, and the hadith is munkar with this isnad. End of his words verbatim.

Al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him, said in *Nayl al-Awtar* concerning this hadith: In its isnad is Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, whom Abu Hatim declared a liar.

Al-Bayhaqi said: I do not know him, and the hadith is munkar with this isnad. It was also narrated by Abu al-Fath al-Azdi in *al-Du'afa'*, and by al-Tabarani in *al-Kabir* through another route from Abu Musa, in which is Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal al-Bajali, who is unknown.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi also recorded it in his *Musnad* from him. End of his words.

Those who hold this view also argued by analogy (qiyas) of sodomy to fornication, with the common ground that both are the insertion of a private part into a private part that is forbidden by the Law and desired by nature.

This was refuted on the basis that analogy does not apply to the fixed penalties (hudud), because they are averted by doubts. But most scholars hold that analogy is permissible in the hudud, and this is the view adopted in *Maraqi al-Su'ud* in the words:

"The hadd and the expiation: estimation (of their ruling by analogy) is permissible, and this is the well-known view."

However, the analogy of the one who commits sodomy to the fornicator is vitiated by the defect called "fasad al-i'tibar" (invalidity of the comparison), because it contradicts the hadith of Ibn Abbas mentioned earlier, that the doer and the one to whom it is done are killed absolutely, whether married or not. There is no doubt that a person of sound nature does not desire sodomy, but rather recoils from it with the utmost revulsion by his nature, as is well known.

The third view: that the one who commits sodomy is not killed, nor is he subjected to the hadd penalty for fornication, but is only disciplined (ta'zir) by beating, imprisonment, and the like. This is the view of Abu Hanifah.

Those who hold this view argued that the Companions disagreed about it, and their disagreement indicates that there is no sound explicit text concerning it, and that it is a matter of independent reasoning (ijtihad), and the hudud are averted by doubts. They said: The term zina does not cover it, because each of them has a specific name of its own, as the poet said:

"From the hand of a free woman dressed as a man, she has two lovers: a sodomite and a fornicator."

They said: It is not valid to join it to zina, because there is a distinguishing factor between them: the motive for zina exists on both sides, unlike sodomy; and zina leads to confusion of lineage and corruption of the marital bed, unlike sodomy. In *Maraqi al-Su'ud* it says: "The distinction between the original case and the derived case is a disqualification: a distinguishing feature specific to the original case that is suitable, or a barrier in the derived case..." etc.

Those who hold this view also argued with the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the two of you who commit it, harm them both﴾ [al-Nisa': 16], the verse.

They said: What is meant by this is sodomy, and what is meant by harm is insulting or beating with sandals.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning "And the two of you who commit it," that he said: "The two men who do it."

Adam and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying "harm them both," that he meant insulting, as mentioned by the author of *al-Durr al-Manthur*.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 88:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in that which I forbid you from﴾, etc. (the verse).

In this noble verse, Allah, may He be exalted, relates about His Prophet Shu'ayb, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, that he informed his people that when he forbade them from something, he himself refrained from it, and that his action did not contradict his speech.

It is understood from this noble verse that a person is obligated to refrain from what he forbids others from, and to comply with what he commands others to do.

Allah has explained this in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Do you order righteousness of the people and forget yourselves while you recite the Scripture?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:44), and His saying: ﴿Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ (al-Saff 61:3).

In the Sahihayn (the two authentic collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown into the Fire, and his intestines will spill out in the Fire, and he will go around with them as a donkey goes around with its millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, did you not used to command us to do good and forbid us from evil?' He will say: 'I used to command you to do good and not do it myself, and I used to forbid you from evil and do it myself.'"

The Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "his intestines will spill out" (fatandaliqu aqtabuhu) means: his bowels will hang down.

Waki', Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym in "al-Hilyah," Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in "Shu'ab al-Iman," and others transmitted from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I saw men whose lips were being cut with scissors of fire. Whenever they were cut, they returned. I said to Jibril: 'Who are these?' He said: 'These are preachers from your nation who used to command people to righteousness and forget themselves, while they recited the Book. Do they not understand?'" This was related by the author of "al-Durr al-Manthur." End of quotation. The poet said:

*Do not forbid a trait while you yourself practice its like; it is a grave shame upon you when you do it.*

One who excelled said:

*And a person who is not pious commanding people to piety is a physician who treats people while he himself is ill.*

It is well known that a person's acting upon what he advises others to do makes others more inclined to accept it from him, as the poet said:

*For if you do not do what you yourself command, you will find that those you command will be doing the same as you do.*

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 91:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed, we see you as weak among us. And were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty against us."﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, exalted is He, makes clear that His Prophet Shu'ayb, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, was protected by Allah from the disbelievers, and his side was strengthened because of tribal sentiments (al-'awatif al-'asabiyyah) and blood ties (al-awasir al-nasabiyyah) from his people, who were disbelievers.

This is evidence that the one who holds fast to his religion may be aided by Allah and strengthened through the support of a disbelieving relative, as He made clear in other places, such as His saying concerning Salih and his people: ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night, and then we will say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family.'"﴾ [An-Naml: 49], and so on.

Thus in the verse there is evidence that they had no power to do evil to Salih, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, except in a state of concealment, and that if they had done this to him secretly and stealthily, they would have sworn to his allies, who were his clan, that they had not done him any harm, nor had they witnessed it or been present for it, out of fear of his clan. So he was mighty in standing because of his disbelieving clan. Allah, exalted is He, said to our Prophet ﷺ: (p-199) ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾ [Ad-Duha: 6], meaning: He gave you refuge by placing you under the care of your uncle Abu Talib.

This was because of tribal sentiments and blood ties, with no connection to religion whatsoever. So His being exalted and bestowing favor upon His Messenger ﷺ by giving him refuge through Abu Talib is evidence that Allah may bestow blessing upon the one who holds fast to his religion through the support of a disbelieving relative.

Among the fruits of that tribal kinship sentiment is the saying of Abu Talib:

"By Allah, they will not reach you with their gathering until I am laid down in the dust, buried."

"So proclaim your command; there is no shame upon you in it. Rejoice in that and let your eyes be cooled by it."

And his saying also:

"And we shall protect him until we are struck down around him, and we forget our sons and our wives."

For this reason, when the Prophet of Allah Lot, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, had no clan among his people to whom he was sent, the effect of having no clan appeared in him, as evidenced by His saying concerning him: ﴿He said, "If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a strong support."﴾ [Hud: 80].

These Quranic verses indicate that Muslims may benefit from the tribal sentiment of their disbelieving brethren.

When the Banu al-Muttalib ibn 'Abd Manaf supported the Banu Hashim, and the Banu 'Abd Shams ibn 'Abd Manaf and the Banu Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf did not support them, the Prophet ﷺ acknowledged to the Banu al-Muttalib that support, which is a tribal kinship sentiment with no connection to religion, so he gave them a share of the fifth of the spoils together with the Banu Hashim, and said: "Verily, we and the Banu al-Muttalib have not been separated in the Jahiliyyah or in Islam." He withheld from the Banu 'Abd Shams and the Banu Nawfal a share of the fifth of the spoils, even though all of them are sons of 'Abd Manaf ibn Qusayy.

Abu Talib said concerning the Banu 'Abd Shams and the Banu Nawfal:

"May Allah repay us regarding 'Abd Shams and Nawfal with a punishment of evil, swift and not delayed."

"By a scale of justice that does not deviate a barleycorn, having a witness from its own self, not in need of supporters."

"Indeed, the intellects of a people have been made foolish, who exchanged for us the sons of Khalaf and the Ghayatil."

"Al-Ghayatil" (with the letter ghayn pointed) refers, in Abu Talib's usage, to the Banu Sahm ibn 'Amr ibn Husays ibn Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy, the well-known tribe among the tribes of Quraysh. They were called al-Ghayatil because Qays ibn 'Adi ibn Sa'd ibn Sahm, who was among the great chiefs of Quraysh, is the one 'Abd al-Muttalib meant when he used to bounce his son 'Abd Allah while he was small, saying:

"As if he, in might, were Qays ibn 'Adi, in the house of Sa'd, who gathers the people of generosity."

(p-200) He had married a woman from Kinanah named "al-Ghaytalah," who was the mother of some of his children. So the Banu Sahm were called the Ghayatil, because Qays ibn 'Adi mentioned was their chief.

These Quranic verses indicate that Allah may aid the believer through the disbeliever because of his partisanship for him, and perhaps there was a good effect from that upon Islam and the Muslims. It may also be one of the favors of Allah upon some of His messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all. In the Sahih, it is related from him ﷺ that he said: "Verily Allah supports this religion through the immoral man." And in the proverb: "Pick the fruits and cast the wood into the fire."

Once you know the indication of the Quran that a Muslim may benefit from a kinship bond and partisanship from a disbeliever, know that calling upon tribal bonds is not permissible, by the consensus of the Muslims that a Muslim may not call out "O people of so-and-so" or the like.

It is established in Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning that call: "Leave it, for it is foul." His saying ﷺ, "Leave it," indicates the obligation of abandoning it, because the form "fa'al" (imperative) is for obligation unless there is a diverting evidence, and there is no diverting evidence here. This is reinforced by his ﷺ giving as the reason for the command to abandon it that it is foul. The Prophet ﷺ did not explicitly command its abandonment and state that it is foul without it being impermissible for anyone to engage in it. What is obligatory upon the Muslims is to call upon the bond of Islam, which, because of its great strength, makes the whole Islamic society as if it were the body of a single person; it binds you to your Muslim brother as the binding of your limbs to one another. He ﷺ said: "The likeness of the believers in their mercy, their love, and their compassion for one another is like the likeness of a single body; when one of its limbs complains, the rest of the body responds to it with wakefulness and fever."

When you reflect upon His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kindred﴾ [Al-Mujadilah: 22], you will realize that kinship bonds vanish in the presence of Islamic bonds. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 10], and He said: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies of one another﴾ [At-Tawbah: 71].

It is not unknown that our predecessors, the community of Muslims, conquered the lands and founded the cities only through the Islamic bond, not through partisan bonds or kinship ties.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 107:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ — the verse.

Allah, exalted is He, restricted the abiding of the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire by the exception of the Will, saying of each of them: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 107]. Then He clarified the absence of cessation in each of them. He said regarding the abiding of the people of Paradise: ﴿a gift that will not be cut off﴾ (p-201) [Hud: 108].

And He said regarding the abiding of the people of the Fire: ﴿Every time its fire abates, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra': 97].

It is known that kullama (whenever) necessarily implies repetition, by the repetition of the action that follows it.

We have explained this matter in full clarity in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), in surah al-An'am in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: The Fire is your abode, abiding therein, except what Allah wills﴾ [al-An'am: 128], and in surah al-Naba' in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Remaining therein for ages﴾ [al-Naba': 23].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ — the verse.

The manner of reconciling it with the verses that are thought to contradict it has already been explained, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Nisa': 57], in surah "al-An'am," and further clarification of it will come, Allah willing, in surah "al-Naba'."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 118:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will not cease to differ,﴾ ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy. And for that He created them.﴾

The scholars differed regarding what is referred to by His saying "that" (dhalika). It was said: ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy,﴾ and "for the mercy He created them." (p-306) The verification is that what is referred to is their difference into wretched and happy, mentioned in His saying: ﴿And they will not cease to differ﴾ ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy.﴾ For that difference He created them, so He created a group for the Garden and a group for the Blaze, as He stated explicitly in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾ (the verse) [al-A'raf: 179]. The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their Sahihs, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "Then Allah sends to it an angel, who is commanded with four words: he writes its provision, its term, its deeds, and whether it is wretched or happy." Muslim related from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "O 'A'ishah! Allah created Paradise and created for it its people, while they were in the loins of their fathers, and He created the Fire and created for it its people, while they were in the loins of their fathers."

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah decreed the measures of creation fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was upon the water."

In the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Each is made easy for that for which he was created."

Since it has been established that His saying: ﴿And for that He created them﴾ means that He created them for the happiness of some and the wretchedness of others, as He said: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell...﴾ (the verse), and He said: ﴿It is He who created you, and among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [al-Taghabun: 2], then the contradiction between these verses and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56] is clearly apparent.

The answer to this is in three aspects:

The first: Ibn Jarir related it from Zayd ibn Aslam and Sufyan that the meaning of the verse, "except that they should worship Me," is: the happy among them worship Me, and the wretched among them disobey Me. Thus the purpose intended by the creation, which is the worship of Allah, is achieved by the act of the happy among them, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿If these disbelieve in it, We have certainly entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾ [al-An'am: 89].

The most that follows from this view is that it applied the whole and intended a part of them, and we have explained similar instances of verses in which the whole is stated while a part is meant, in Surah al-Anfal.

(p-307) The second aspect: it is what Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Jarir preferred it: that the meaning of His saying, "except that they should worship Me," is: except that they should acknowledge servitude to Me, willingly or unwillingly, because the believer obeys by his own choice, while the disbeliever is submissive and compliant to the decree of his Lord under compulsion.

The third aspect, and it appears to me that it is the truth, due to the indication of the Qur'an: the will in His saying, "And for that He created them," is a universal, decreed will (irada kawniyya qadariyya), and the will in His saying, "And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me," is a legislative, religious will (irada shar'iyya dîniyya). In His saying, "And for that He created them," and His saying, "And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind," He clarified that He willed, by His universal decreed will, that some people become happy and others become wretched.

And by His saying, "except that they should worship Me," He clarified that He wills worship from the jinn and mankind by His legislative religious will; so He grants success to whomever He wills by His universal will, and he worships Him, and He forsakes whomever He wills, and he refrains from worship.

The evidence from the Qur'an for this is that He, exalted is He, stated it in His saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 64]. He generalized the legislative will by His saying "except to be obeyed," and clarified the restriction in obedience by the universal will in His saying "by the permission of Allah." So the call is general and the granting of success is specific.

As for establishing the relation between the universal (kawniyya), the decreed (qadariyya), and the legislative religious (shar'iyya dîniyya) wills: with respect to the existence or non-existence of the willed thing, the universal will is more general absolutely, because every thing willed legislatively comes into existence externally when it is willed universally and decreed, such as the faith of Abu Bakr, while nothing exists that was not willed universally and decreed, even if it was willed legislatively, such as the faith of Abu Lahab. So every legislatively willed thing that occurs does so by the universal will, and not every universally willed thing occurs as something willed in the law.

With respect to the relation of the two wills to the worship of jinn and mankind to Allah, the legislative will is more general absolutely and the universal will is more specific absolutely, because every individual of the jinn and mankind has been willed by Allah to worship Him legislatively, but He did not will it of all of them universally and by decree. Thus the legislative will encompasses the worship of all of both kinds, while the universal will is restricted to the worship of the happy among them, as we have previously mentioned, that the call is general and the granting of success is specific, as He stated, exalted is He, in His saying: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus: 25]. He explicitly stated that He calls all, and guides whomever He wills among them.

The relation between the legislative and the decreed wills is not one of general and specific from one aspect; rather they are (p-308) absolutely general and specific, as we have explained, though one of them is more general than the other absolutely in one respect, and the second is more general absolutely in another respect, as we have explained. And Allah knows best.
